## Overview

We fit a Bayesian occupancy model to estimate the position of the cane toad invasion front in each year. The model combines two types of survey data collected across multiple years: nocturnal time-to-detection (TTD) surveys, and fixed-effort visual count surveys (Clulow et al.). Both data types are linked through a common encounter rate parameter $\lambda$ and a shared geometric model of the invasion front.

We index years with $k$, and individual observations with $i$ (TTD surveys) or $j$ (count surveys).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Occupancy model

We model the invasion front as a straight line in two-dimensional space (projected coordinates, Albers equal-area, centred and scaled to km):

$$y_k = ax + b_k$$

where $a$ is a slope shared across all years and $b_k$ is a year-specific intercept. The perpendicular (signed) distance from observation site $(x, y)$ to the year-$k$ front is:

$$d_{ik} = \frac{y_i - ax_i - b_k}{\sqrt{1+a^2}}$$

Occupancy — whether toads are present at a site — is a deterministic step function of this distance. Sites on the toad side of the front ($d_{ik} \geq 0$) are occupied; sites beyond the front ($d_{ik} < 0$) are not:

$$H(d_{ik}) = \begin{cases} 1 & d_{ik} \geq 0 \\ 0 & d_{ik} < 0 \end{cases}$$

This deterministic occupancy assumption is appropriate given the highly aggregated nature of the invasion and the relatively coarse spatial scale of the analysis.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detection model

All survey types share a common toad encounter rate $\lambda$ (toads detected per person-minute), which parameterises detection probability under a Poisson encounter process. The three survey types each contribute a different observation likelihood.

### Nocturnal TTD surveys

For nocturnal visual surveys, observers search until the first toad is detected and record the elapsed person-minutes at that point. Under a Poisson encounter process with rate $\lambda$, the time to first detection $t^d_i$ follows an exponential distribution:

$$t^d_i \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$$

For surveys with a detection, $t^d_i$ is observed directly. For surveys with no detection, $t^d_i$ is treated as a latent variable — the sampler integrates over all values consistent with the exponential prior and the observed non-detection.

The probability of at least one detection during a survey of total duration $t^v_i$, given presence, is:

$$P(\text{detect} \mid \text{present}) = 1 - e^{-\lambda t^v_i}$$

The binary detection outcome $o_i$ is therefore:

$$o_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(H(d_{ik}) \cdot \left[1 - e^{-\lambda t^v_i}\right]\right)$$

### Fixed-effort count surveys (Clulow)

A separate dataset (Clulow et al.) consists of standardised visual surveys in which two observers searched independently for 15 minutes (total effort $T_j = 30$ person-minutes), recording the total number of toads seen. Under the same Poisson encounter process, the expected count given presence is $\lambda T_j$, so:

$$c_j \sim \text{Poisson}\!\left(H(d_{jk}) \cdot T_j \cdot \lambda\right)$$

This is consistent with the TTD likelihood: both are derived from a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$. The exponential TTD distribution arises from the waiting time to the first event of this process, while the count distribution arises from the number of events in a fixed window. The count data are therefore complementary to — and share the same $\lambda$ as — the TTD data, while being more informative about $\lambda$ because they capture the full count distribution rather than only whether a toad was detected.

A subset of Clulow sites have only presence/absence records (no count data). For these sites we use the same Bernoulli likelihood as for nocturnal surveys, with effort fixed at $T_j = 30$ person-minutes:

$$o_j \sim \text{Bernoulli}\!\left(H(d_{jk}) \cdot \left[1 - e^{-\lambda T_j}\right]\right)$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Priors

$$\lambda \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)$$ $$a \sim \text{Normal}(0, 10^{-8}) \quad \text{(effectively flat on the scale of interest)}$$ $$b_k \sim \text{Normal}(0, 10^{-4}) \quad \text{(SD} \approx 100 \text{ km)}$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Derived quantities

The perpendicular distance the front moved between year $k$ and year $k+1$ is:

$$\delta_k = \frac{b_{k+1} - b_k}{\sqrt{1+a^2}}$$

Positive values of $\delta_k$ indicate southward (inland) advance; negative values indicate retreat. We report the posterior distribution of $\delta_k$ for each consecutive year pair as a measure of annual front movement.
